issues.legal_issue: A person cannot use fundamental-rights challenges to reopen a shrine’s status as a Sikh place of worship where pre-constitutional law had already declared that status and vested its management in another body.
material_facts: A pre-constitutional ruler’s order declared the shrine to be a Sikh place of worship and vested its management in an interim board.
The order continued to have the force of law after the Constitution came into effect, and the shrine’s management remained with the board through the later legislative transition.
The claimant had not asserted a right to manage the shrine during the relevant period and challenged its status only later.
issues.conclusion: The claimant could not challenge the shrine’s established status on fundamental-rights grounds; the pre-constitutional law had already determined its status and management.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 372, pre-constitutional law continues in force until repealed or replaced by competent legislation. Fundamental rights are not retrospective. The Court relied on Ameerunnissa Begum v. Mahboob Begum and State of Rajasthan v. Shri Sajjanlal Panjawat for the continuing legal force of a ruler’s order, and referred to Sri Jagadguru Kari Basava Rajendraswami of Gavimutt and Seth Shanti Sarup v. Union of India on the non-retrospective operation of fundamental rights.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_shrine_statu: A claimant challenges a shrine’s established religious status on constitutional grounds.
predicates.preconstitutional_law_declared_shrine_st: A law in force before the Constitution came into effect declared the shrine to have the disputed religious status.
predicates.preconstitutional_law_vested_management_: A law in force before the Constitution came into effect vested management of the shrine in a body other than the claimant.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a shrine whose status and management were already determined by pre-constitutional law, the claimant cannot reopen that determination on fundamental-rights grounds.

issues.legal_issue: Legislative provisions making compliance with preliminary steps conclusively proved by publication of a notification are not unconstitutional merely because they prevent a party from contesting those preliminary steps.
material_facts: The challenged provisions made publication of specified notifications conclusive proof that prescribed preliminary requirements had been complied with.
Those requirements concerned steps preceding an inquiry in which the substantive dispute could be determined.
The statutory process was designed to reduce prolonged litigation over places of worship.
For the notification concerning scheduled shrines, the Government was expected to satisfy itself that the application had been properly made before publishing the notification.
issues.conclusion: The conclusive-proof provisions were valid and did not violate the constitutional guarantees invoked by the claimants.
issues.legal_principle: A legislature competent to enact a law may prescribe irrebuttable presumptions as rules of evidence or as substantive law, provided the provisions are not otherwise unconstitutional. A conclusive rule concerning preliminary steps does not itself exercise a judicial function. The Court relied on Municipal Board, Hapur v. Raghuvendra Kripal and referred to Izhar Ahmad Khan v. Union of India. It also held that the requirement that an application be duly forwarded called for the Government to satisfy itself that the relevant application requirements had been met.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_conclusive_n: A party to a proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a rule that gives a notification conclusive effect.
predicates.notification_makes_preliminary_complianc: The governing law makes publication of a notification conclusive proof that specified preliminary procedural requirements were met.
predicates.substantive_inquiry_remains_available: The process still provides an inquiry in which the substantive dispute can be determined.

issues.definition: A rule giving a notification conclusive effect as to preliminary compliance is valid where a substantive inquiry remains available.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot rebut conclusive statutory proof of preliminary procedural compliance by alleging that notice was absent, late, or otherwise defective when that compliance is covered by the conclusive rule.
material_facts: The claimants alleged defects concerning individual notice and other steps taken before publication of a notification.
The governing provision made publication conclusive proof of compliance with the specified procedural steps.
Those steps preceded an inquiry that formed part of the determination of the substantive dispute.
issues.conclusion: Once the conclusive-proof provision was upheld, the covered preliminary compliance could not be reopened by alleging that notice or another preliminary step was defective.
issues.legal_principle: A challenge that would rebut a valid conclusive statutory presumption is inconsistent with the presumption’s conclusive nature. The Court also reasoned that the preliminary steps facilitated the inquiry rather than determined the substantive dispute, and that using challenges to those steps to prolong litigation was not unreasonable. It relied on Municipal Board, Hapur v. Raghuvendra Kripal in upholding the validity of conclusive proof of preliminary steps.

predicates.proceeding_challenges_notification_based: A party in a proceeding challenges a determination initiated by publication of a statutory notification.
predicates.law_makes_preliminary_compliance_conclus: The governing law makes publication conclusive proof that specified preliminary steps were completed.
predicates.objection_concerns_covered_preliminary_s: The party’s objection alleges a defect in a preliminary step covered by the conclusive rule, such as service of notice.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns a notification and the law makes specified preliminary compliance conclusive, an objection to a covered preliminary step cannot reopen that compliance.

issues.legal_issue: The limits on who may challenge a notification as a hereditary office-holder do not make the statutory challenge procedure unconstitutional merely because a possible break in succession could prevent a particular claimant from qualifying.
material_facts: The law allowed a hereditary office-holder to challenge a notification and defined the relevant office by reference to succession through hereditary right or nomination.
The claimant argued that a break in succession or appointment of a successor by a religious congregation could leave a person unable to qualify as a hereditary office-holder.
The law also permitted a group of worshippers to challenge the notification where a hereditary office-holder could not be found.
Whether a claimant qualified as a hereditary office-holder was for the tribunal to decide under the applicable rules of evidence.
issues.conclusion: The asserted succession gap did not establish that the procedure was unconstitutional; a tribunal could determine whether a claimant qualified, and the available worshipper procedure addressed the claimed gap.
issues.legal_principle: The statutory definition included succession by hereditary right or by nomination, and the claimant’s standing was to be determined by the tribunal on the evidence. The Court rejected the asserted exclusion as hypothetical and held that an alternative challenge by worshippers was available where no hereditary office-holder could be found.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_challenger_e: A party challenges the constitutionality of limits on who may bring a statutory challenge.
predicates.challenge_relies_on_possible_succession_: The challenge rests on the possibility that a break in succession or an appointment could leave a claimant unable to qualify as a hereditary office-holder.
predicates.worshipper_challenge_route_available: The process permits a qualifying group of worshippers to bring the challenge if no hereditary office-holder can do so.

issues.definition: A possible succession gap does not make challenger-eligibility limits unconstitutional where worshippers have an alternative route to challenge and the tribunal can decide an individual claimant’s status.

issues.legal_issue: Different statutory procedures for challenging a shrine’s status do not violate equality merely because one procedure is available to an office-holder and another procedure is available in a different kind of proceeding.
material_facts: The claimants argued that the procedure available to a hereditary office-holder was more onerous than the procedure in an ordinary court proceeding.
The statutory scheme provided different routes for challenging the status of a shrine, depending on the circumstances in which the status was disputed.
The Court found no basis to conclude that the difference between those routes violated the claimants’ constitutional rights.
issues.conclusion: The different procedures were not shown to be unconstitutional or discriminatory.
issues.legal_principle: The Court rejected the contention that providing different procedures for the same general purpose, in distinct statutory settings, was by itself discriminatory or an unconstitutional restriction.

predicates.constitutional_equality_challenge_to_dif: A party alleges that differing procedures for challenging the same general matter violate equality.
predicates.procedures_apply_in_distinct_statutory_s: The procedures apply in distinct statutory settings or to different categories of challenger.

issues.definition: Different procedures in distinct settings are not unconstitutional merely because their requirements differ.

issues.legal_issue: A short statutory period for worshippers to challenge a notification is not unreasonable where it gives them sufficient time to organize and pursue the challenge.
material_facts: The law allowed a group of worshippers to challenge a notification within a prescribed period.
The claimants argued that the period was unreasonable.
The Court considered the period sufficient for the required number of worshippers to organize and bring a challenge.
issues.conclusion: The prescribed period was not unreasonable or unconstitutional.
issues.legal_principle: A limitation period is necessarily somewhat arbitrary, and a period is not unconstitutional merely for being fixed; the relevant question includes whether it affords a reasonable opportunity to exercise the right. The Court held that the period was sufficient for the required worshippers to assemble and challenge the notification.

predicates.proceeding_challenges_notification_time_: A party challenges a fixed time limit for bringing a statutory challenge to a notification.
predicates.challengers_must_act_within_fixed_period: The governing process requires the challengers to act within a specified period.
predicates.period_allows_reasonable_opportunity_to_: The period gives the required group of challengers a reasonable opportunity to organize and bring the challenge.

issues.definition: A fixed period for challenging a notification is not unreasonable when it gives the required challengers a reasonable opportunity to organize and act.

issues.legal_issue: A conclusive declaration that a shrine is a Sikh place of worship does not prevent a claimant from asserting that the physical property listed in connection with the shrine belongs to a non-Sikh religious institution.
material_facts: The shrine was included in a statutory schedule and a notification declared it to be a Sikh place of worship.
The claimant was identified as being in possession of property listed in connection with the shrine and sought to claim that the property belonged to an Udasi institution.
The respondents accepted that a claim could be made concerning the listed property, including the property described as the shrine itself.
Earlier interpretations of the statutory scheme permitted claims to the physical property while distinguishing such claims from a claim to the shrine as a religious institution.
issues.conclusion: In Khanna J.’s concurring opinion, the statutory declaration did not bar a claim that the listed physical property, including the shrine building, belonged to an Udasi institution; on that construction, the provision did not violate the claimant’s rights.
issues.legal_principle: Khanna J. relied on the presumption of constitutional validity, the longstanding construction of the local enactment, and the interpretations in the Sikh Gurdwara Tribunal’s order concerning Gurdwara Rupar and Mahant Davinder Singh v. Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. He also referred to Raj Narain Pandey v. Sant Prasad Tewari on adhering to a settled interpretation of a local statute.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_conclusive_s: A party challenges the constitutionality of a conclusive declaration about a shrine’s religious status.
predicates.claimant_asserts_property_belongs_to_dif: The claimant asserts that the physical property listed in connection with the shrine belongs to a different religious institution.
predicates.property_claim_remains_adjudicable: The statutory process permits the tribunal to adjudicate the claimant’s property claim despite the declaration.

issues.definition: A conclusive declaration about a shrine’s religious status does not bar a claim to the associated physical property where that property claim remains open for adjudication.
